content: Breast engorgement occurs when an excessive amount of breast milk accumulates within the mammary glands. This condition is typically caused by insufficient breastfeeding or blocked milk ducts. When the breasts become engorged, they may swell, throb, and cause varying degrees of pain, ranging from mild to severe. If left untreated, engorgement can lead to mastitis, which is an inflammation of the breast tissue. Additionally, the pressure from untreated engorgement can obstruct milk ducts, resulting in a plugged duct. Women experiencing this may notice a lump in a specific area of the breast, and the skin over that area may appear red and feel warm to the touch. If the condition progresses unchecked, the plugged duct can develop into a breast infection, which may present with symptoms such as fever or flu-like illness. To manage breast engorgement, it is crucial to continue breastfeeding frequently, even though it may seem counterintuitive. Regular nursing helps to reduce milk levels and prevent further complications. It is generally beneficial to breastfeed often to keep the breasts as empty as possible, although a lactating breast is never completely empty. Treatment for engorgement, plugged ducts, and infections involves frequent nursing to drain the breast effectively. Applying wet heat and performing gentle massage—starting from the engorged or lumpy areas and moving toward the nipple—before nursing can also be helpful. Additionally, positioning the baby so that their chin points toward the most affected area of the breast can aid in clearing the blockage. If the condition has progressed to mastitis, it is important to ensure adequate nutrition and hydration. Bed rest and frequent nursing, with no more than two hours between the start of one feeding and the next, are essential. If a breast infection is left untreated or inadequately managed, it can develop into a breast abscess, which may require surgical drainage. Any breast infection that persists for more than 24 hours or becomes severe should be promptly reported to a healthcare provider, as antibiotics may be necessary. It is also important to note that a rare but serious form of breast cancer, known as inflammatory breast cancer, can present with symptoms similar to mastitis, including breast swelling. This type of cancer has been reported in breastfeeding women and is the most aggressive form of breast cancer, with the highest mortality rate. It is often not detectable through mammography or ultrasound. If mastitis or a breast abscess does not improve after two weeks of antibiotic therapy, a physician should evaluate the possibility of inflammatory breast cancer.
